what-happens-when-you-put-a-rainbow-in-a.title: What Happens When You Put a Rainbow in an Oven?
what-happens-when-you-put-a-rainbow-in-a.description: What is glass fusion? Discover how colorful glass becomes kiln-fired art, why beginners love it, and where to try a fused-glass class in Chicago or Eugene.
what-happens-when-you-put-a-rainbow-in-a.subtitle: A colorful introduction to the oddly satisfying world of fused glass.
what-happens-when-you-put-a-rainbow-in-a.imageAlt: Hand-drawn kiln with colored glass shapes transforming into a rainbow
what-happens-when-you-put-a-rainbow-in-a.html:
You know the feeling: you see a tray of tiny, jewel-colored pieces and think, I could play with those for hours. Now imagine arranging them into a little picture—and letting a kiln finish what your imagination started.

That’s glass fusion. It's part collage, part color experiment, and part dramatic makeover. The before photo is cute. The after photo is the one that makes people ask, “Wait, you MADE that?”

First, one important clarification: not that kind of oven

Despite the title, this is absolutely not a project for your kitchen oven. Glass fusion uses a specialized, programmable kiln. Your home oven makes lasagna. A glass kiln helps compatible glass pieces soften and join into one artwork. Everybody has a lane.

At Color Cocktail Factory, the fun begins at the table: choosing colors, testing combinations, arranging shapes, and deciding when a piece finally feels like yours. Trained staff take care of firing and controlled cooling afterward.

The three acts of a tiny glass drama

Act I: The audition. A clear base meets little pieces of blue, amber, coral, and green glass. There is no correct color choice. You can make a sunrise or a tiny abstract painting that looks like jazz sounds.

Act II: The transformation. The assembled work goes into a kiln. Heat allows compatible glass pieces to bond. Depending on the firing technique, the finished surface may keep some texture or soften into smooth shapes.

Act III: The reveal. After careful cooling, what began as separate pieces has become a single piece of glass art. Light passes through the transparent areas and catches its edges. Suddenly your miniature masterpiece has a second personality.

The only suspense we enjoy more than a good movie ending is opening a cooled glass kiln.

But do I need to know how to draw?

Not even a little. You can work with blocks of color, circles, simple lines, or repeating patterns. In fact, glass often looks especially beautiful when a design is simple enough to let the light do some of the work.

Try this idea: pick one hero color, one friend for it, and one tiny surprise. Blue, turquoise, and a little orange? Lovely. Pink, red, and one outrageous yellow square? Absolutely.

And no, fused glass isn't stained glass or glassblowing. It is its own technique: the design is laid out with compatible solid glass pieces, then joined with kiln heat.

What happens in a CCF glass-fusion class?

You get a guided creative experience with materials and help at the table. The exact artwork, duration, and price depend on the session you select; check the live listing for those details. Your finished work is kiln-fired after the class, so you’ll return for pickup once it is ready.

The best part isn't that everyone follows the same instructions. It's that everyone starts with colors and finishes with a completely different idea.

Ready to make light do something interesting? See Glass Fusion in Chicago or explore the Eugene Glass Fusion class page to check availability.

Tiny FAQ before you go

Is this good for a first-time maker? Yes—check the beginner level on your chosen class and follow the instructor’s guidance.

Do I take it home immediately? No. The glass needs a kiln firing and controlled cooling before pickup.

Can I bring a friend? Definitely. Choosing colors side by side is half the entertainment.

wonderful-science-of-melting-glass.title: The Wonderful Science of Melting Glass
wonderful-science-of-melting-glass.description: Explore the simple science of glass fusion: tack fuse versus full fuse, color changes, compatible glass, and kiln cooling—without the intimidating jargon.
wonderful-science-of-melting-glass.subtitle: A very unofficial lab notebook about heat, color, and glass that behaves itself.
wonderful-science-of-melting-glass.imageAlt: Hand-drawn three-stage diagram of arranging, heating, and annealing glass
wonderful-science-of-melting-glass.html:
Lab note 01: Glass is a fascinating material because it can look perfectly solid on your table and behave very differently in a hot kiln. Which is mildly rude of it—and excellent for art.

Here are five questions that make glass fusion much more interesting once you know the answers.

Question 01 / Is the glass actually melting?

Think softening and flowing, not cartoon lava. As glass gets hotter, it becomes less viscous and can bond with neighboring pieces. A tack fuse joins pieces while preserving more of their shape and texture. A full fuse encourages them to flow together more smoothly.

The result depends on the glass, the arrangement, the kiln, and the firing schedule. This is why instructors test designs instead of offering a one-temperature-fits-all recipe.

Question 02 / Why can't I use random glass from my recycling bin?

Because beautiful pieces of glass can be deeply incompatible roommates. Different glasses expand and contract at different rates. Put mismatched pieces together, and internal stress can leave the finished artwork fragile or cracked.

For kilnwork, studios use manufacturer-tested compatible fusible glass, not mystery fragments collected from kitchen bottles. Even matching COE numbers alone does not guarantee compatibility across brands.

Question 03 / Why does the color sometimes change?

Glass color can come from minerals and metallic compounds. Cobalt famously creates many blues; iron can create greens. Some art-glass colors also strike during firing, developing a stronger or different color after heatwork.

In other words, a piece that looks shy on the table can leave the kiln behaving like a disco ball. The studio uses tested materials and examples so the surprise remains enjoyable.

Question 04 / Why can't we open the kiln right away?

Meet the least glamorous and most important part of glass fusion: annealing. Hot glass must cool in a controlled way so that temperature differences don't create damaging internal stresses.

The kiln is not merely cooking the artwork. It is also helping it cool safely. Imagine baking a cake that gets ruined if you open the door too early, except the cake is glass and significantly less edible.

Question 05 / Is glass fusion the same as glassblowing?

No. In glassblowing, an artist gathers hot, softened glass and shapes it with tools and often air. In glass fusion, you usually assemble a composition first, then place it in a kiln to join the pieces. One feels like a performance at a furnace; the other begins like a colorful tabletop puzzle.

The very short experiment you can do safely

Find three transparent colored objects around your home—a tinted bottle, a plastic folder, or even colored cellophane. Look at each near a window, then overlap two and see how the transmitted colors change. You are not fusing anything. You're just noticing that light is an active part of the design.

For the real kiln transformation, leave the heat to trained professionals.

Your lab invitation

If you like science best when you can make something with it, try a guided class. Start with the Chicago glass-fusion booking page or visit Glass Fusion in Eugene for current availability. You bring curiosity; the studio brings the compatible glass and the kiln.

Final lab result: science + color + a little patience = something worth putting in the window.

ten-beautiful-things-to-make-with-fused-.title: 10 Beautiful Things You Can Make With Fused Glass
ten-beautiful-things-to-make-with-fused-.description: Discover 10 fused-glass project ideas, from suncatchers and ornaments to tiny art panels, and get inspired to try a beginner-friendly glass workshop.
ten-beautiful-things-to-make-with-fused-.subtitle: Small projects, enormous personality. Consider this your permission slip to play.
ten-beautiful-things-to-make-with-fused-.imageAlt: Illustrated gallery of colorful handmade-style small glass objects
ten-beautiful-things-to-make-with-fused-.html:
You don’t need to plan a giant sculpture. Some of the most charming glass projects fit in the palm of your hand. Here are ten ideas to steal—artistically speaking.

A note from the studio: This is an inspiration gallery, not a promise that all ten projects are offered in one class. Size, shapes, materials, and finishing options vary. Check your selected session for its actual project.

01. The tiny sunset

A clear panel, a warm orange circle, and one soft pink horizon. Put it near daylight and watch the mood change with the weather. You don't need an entire landscape to suggest one.

02. A pocket-size abstract painting

Make a color-block composition with three rectangles and one rebellious triangle. Try a Bauhaus-inspired layout, or make up your own geometry. Consider it modern art with fewer museum guards.

03. The botanical suncatcher

Little green leaves, a blue sky, and one oversized flower. A gentle theme for people who can never keep plants alive but still deserve something beautiful in the window.

04. The constellation ornament

A dark-blue base with light, starry dots creates a tiny night sky. It can work as a hanging decoration when the piece is designed and finished with suitable hardware.

05. The miniature landscape

Three horizontal bands make a sea, a mountain, and a strange new planet—depending on how adventurous your colors are. Glass rewards the art of leaving things out.

06. A sparkling pendant

A small composition can become a piece of jewelry with the right finishing process, hardware, and edge treatment. Think less “diamond necklace,” more “I made a little piece of the ocean.”

07. The garden color marker

Turn a small glass design into garden art with proper outdoor-safe mounting. Even a single bright rectangle can look wonderful against green leaves.

08. A cheerful little wall panel

Choose a bold symbol, striped pattern, or abstract doodle and make something that belongs beside a bookshelf or near a doorway.

09. The tiny jewelry dish

A fused-glass blank can sometimes be slumped in a separate firing over a mold to create a shallow dish. This is a more advanced finishing step, not something every beginner class includes. Decorative use is simplest; food-contact suitability must be specifically verified.

10. The gift with a secret meaning

Make a design built around someone's favorite colors, initials, a shared trip, or an inside joke. You might see a cluster of shapes; your friend sees the summer you spent by the lake.

Can't choose? Try the three-color rule

Pick one dominant color, one supporting color, and one tiny accent. Give them enough room to breathe. This simple constraint makes a beginner design feel intentional without turning it into homework.

Start with one piece

At Color Cocktail Factory, you can try a guided glass-fusion class and make a project based on that session’s materials and format. Find Chicago Glass Fusion dates or check the Eugene Glass Fusion page.

You don't have to make all ten things. You only need to make the first one.

from-ancient-rome-to-your-kitchen-window.title: From Ancient Rome to Your Kitchen Window
from-ancient-rome-to-your-kitchen-window.description: Travel through the history of colorful glass: ancient mosaic glass, Roman innovations, stained glass windows, and today’s kiln-fused artwork.
from-ancient-rome-to-your-kitchen-window.subtitle: A whirlwind, wonderfully colorful history of humans making things out of glass.
from-ancient-rome-to-your-kitchen-window.imageAlt: Hand-drawn timeline of ancient glass, mosaics, windows and modern glass art
from-ancient-rome-to-your-kitchen-window.html:
Imagine walking into a museum after hours. The lights turn on one room at a time, and every room tells the same story: humans have always been a little obsessed with making sand turn into beauty.

Glass fusion is part of that very long conversation. Let's take the express tour. Comfortable shoes optional; time machine hypothetical.

Stop 1 — Ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt: glass is a luxury

Humans were making glass thousands of years ago. The Corning Museum of Glass traces human-made glass back roughly 4,000 years to Mesopotamia. Early glass objects could be cast or shaped around a core. Glass was precious, colorful, and often saved for jewelry, ornaments, perfume containers, and the powerful.

If you owned a vivid little glass object back then, you probably weren't tossing it into a kitchen drawer beside three spare phone chargers.

Stop 2 — The Hellenistic world: tiny pieces, big patterns

By the third century BCE, mosaic glass techniques had become increasingly popular around the Mediterranean. Craftspeople arranged pieces or patterned glass canes and fused them into extraordinary decorative objects.

Some ancient mosaic glass is so intricate that it looks digitally designed. It wasn't. It was patience, heat, and astonishing hand skills.

Today's tabletop fusing class isn't identical to ancient mosaic-glass production, but there is a lovely family resemblance: arrange color, use heat, reveal an object that couldn't exist as loose pieces.

Stop 3 — The Romans: now everybody wants glass

Glassblowing emerged in the eastern Mediterranean around the first century BCE and spread widely in the Roman world. Suddenly, glass vessels could be made more efficiently. Everyday cups and containers became more common, alongside spectacular luxury pieces.

Glassblowing and glass fusion are different techniques, but the Roman story shows how quickly an invention can change what people expect from a material.

Stop 4 — Medieval windows: color goes monumental

Stained-glass windows turned sunlight into architecture. Unlike kiln-fused glass pieces, traditional leaded windows usually hold separate colored pieces together with metal strips. Still, the visual lesson is universal: color changes when light becomes part of the artwork.

A window can look still on a cloudy morning and glorious at sunset. The wall hasn't moved. The light has.

Stop 5 — The studio-glass era: artists take the wheel

The twentieth century saw renewed experimentation with glass as an independent artistic medium. In the United States, the Studio Glass movement took off in 1962; many artists started exploring glass on a more intimate, experimental scale. Kilnforming remained one of several approaches artists could use to work with color and form.

The history isn't a straight line from an ancient bowl to today's craft table. It's more like a brilliant, branching family tree.

Final stop — Your own little glass artwork

And now here you are, choosing colors in a studio instead of standing inside a museum. You do not need to invent a Roman technique, master a medieval trade, or explain 3,000 years of art history to make something interesting.

You only need an idea and a willingness to try.

Join a guided Color Cocktail Factory class in Chicago, or explore Eugene Glass Fusion for availability. A tiny handmade piece can be a new chapter in a very old love story.

handmade-glass-gifts-with-a-story.title: Why Handmade Glass Makes a Better Gift Than Another Candle
handmade-glass-gifts-with-a-story.description: Looking for a creative handmade gift? See why a fused-glass keepsake or glass-art workshop experience makes a thoughtful, personal surprise.
handmade-glass-gifts-with-a-story.subtitle: An extremely friendly argument for gifts with fingerprints and good stories.
handmade-glass-gifts-with-a-story.imageAlt: Minimal hand-drawn gift box with a colorful glass artwork gift tag
handmade-glass-gifts-with-a-story.html:
The case: You want to give someone a gift. They're delightful. You care about them. They also already own approximately 46 mugs and enough scented candles to illuminate a small medieval castle.

The court will now consider the evidence for a different kind of present: a handmade piece of glass art.

Exhibit A: “I made this for you” is a surprisingly powerful sentence

A store-bought gift says, “I thought of you.” A handmade gift can add, “I spent an afternoon experimenting, made a few questionable color decisions, and kept going because this reminded me of you.”

That doesn't mean handmade automatically wins. It means the story becomes part of the present.

Imagine a small glass panel inspired by a friend's love of the ocean. Maybe it's just layered blues and a little flash of gold. They see their favorite place; you see an afternoon well spent. Both are true.

Exhibit B: Glass changes its appearance with the light

A colorful glass piece can feel different at 9 AM and 5 PM. Sunlight, shadows, and where you place it all become part of the design. Not every gift gets a daily wardrobe change without asking you to buy accessories.

Exhibit C: It doesn't have to match the furniture

Handmade glass is allowed to be a little strange. It can be cheerful, asymmetrical, abstract, or almost ridiculously colorful. A sentimental object rarely needs to win a minimalist interior-design contest.

A small glass artwork can live near a window, on a shelf, or as a carefully mounted decoration, depending on the finished piece.

An important note from the candle defense team

We actually love candles. Color Cocktail Factory teaches creative workshops, including candle making. This is not an anti-candle manifesto. It is simply a reminder that when a loved one's candle shelf reaches capacity, you are allowed to try a new direction.

The best gift might be the afternoon itself

Instead of guessing someone's taste, you can give them the experience of choosing the colors themselves. Go together, bring a friend, or turn it into a creative date. A glass-fusion class is an activity and a future keepsake rolled into one.

And if you're making the gift rather than giving the experience, remember that glass takes time in the kiln. Plan for pickup after firing, not an instant take-home surprise. Check the current session for exact timing and what is included.

The verdict

There is no universally best present. But there is something lovely about making an object for a person who will understand why you picked those colors.

Case closed. With a tiny sparkle.

why-we-cannot-stop-looking-at-colored-gl.title: Why We Can’t Stop Looking at Colored Glass
why-we-cannot-stop-looking-at-colored-gl.description: Why is colored glass so mesmerizing? Explore the art of transparency, reflected light, and colorful glass designs, then try creating your own.
why-we-cannot-stop-looking-at-colored-gl.subtitle: A tiny love letter to sunlight, windows, and color that refuses to sit still.
why-we-cannot-stop-looking-at-colored-gl.imageAlt: Hand-drawn window with hanging colored glass shapes casting rays of color
why-we-cannot-stop-looking-at-colored-gl.html:
There is a moment in the afternoon when the sun slips through a colored window and ordinary walls stop behaving like ordinary walls.

A blue patch travels across the floor. A warm amber shape lands on a book. The room hasn't changed its furniture, but somehow it has changed its mood.

This is what colored glass does so beautifully: it gives light somewhere interesting to go.

The first look: color that doesn't sit still

Paint can be wonderfully rich, but glass has an extra collaborator. Some light reflects from its surface; some travels through it; some is absorbed. Clear, transparent, translucent, and opaque glasses all behave differently.

A little glass panel held in front of a white wall can look completely different from the same panel held near a bright window. The artwork is not performing a trick. You are seeing the material's relationship with light.

The second look: two colors become a conversation

Place a transparent blue piece over a transparent yellow one and you may see an unexpected new color where the light passes through both. Put an opaque piece in the mix and you change the whole composition again.

Glass color comes from chemistry as well as design. Materials such as cobalt and iron can give glass characteristic colors, while some specialty art glass develops its final appearance during firing.

If that sounds complicated, here's the simplest version: glass is a color experiment you can hang in a window.

The third look: the shapes are only half the picture

Try a tiny exercise next time you see a colored glass object:

At arm's length: Notice the large shapes first. Which color speaks loudest?

At the window: Watch how the transparent parts change. Where does the light seem brightest?

Two steps away: Look for the overall mood. Is the piece calm, energetic, playful, or unexpectedly dramatic?

There are no wrong answers. In design, your eye is part of the equipment.

Why simple compositions can feel so sophisticated

A square of blue, a thin line of orange, a generous area of clear glass. That is enough to make something striking. Negative space—the parts you leave open—gives the eye somewhere to rest and sunlight somewhere to travel.

This is wonderful news if you're a beginner. You don't need to draw a realistic flower or invent an elaborate pattern. Start with three colors and one feeling: warm, peaceful, joyful, stormy, whatever is yours today.

A small invitation to make color tangible

In a guided fused-glass workshop, you arrange compatible glass pieces into a composition, and trained staff handle the kiln work afterward. What you make will be your own little study in light and color, finished after careful firing and cooling.

Explore Glass Fusion in Chicago or visit Eugene Glass Fusion to see current availability and project details.

You may arrive thinking you're making a piece of glass. You may leave thinking a little differently about every sunny window you pass.
